description: The VAPP Act came into force on 25 May 2015 and is the first federal law attempting to prohibit FGM nationally - but as a federal law it is directly effective only in the Federal Capital Territory. Thirteen states have their own express prohibitions: Lagos, Osun, Ondo, Ekiti, Bayelsa, Ogun, Delta, Ebonyi, Oyo, Imo, Edo, Cross River and Rivers.
energy_note: Banned nationally, in a way that binds one territory.

description: Highest prevalence in the South-East and South-West, lowest in the North-East. Types I and II are most common; types III and IV are also carried out, particularly in northern parts.

aspect: The law has not yet reversed it for girls
description: Prevalence decreased among women aged 15-49 but rose among girls, from 16.9% in 2013 to 19.2% in 2018, despite the 2015 ban. And because the population is growing, the absolute number of girls cut is increasing even where rates fall.
energy_note: The rate fell for women and rose for girls.

aspect: The generational signal is real though
description: Analysis across MICS rounds from 2007 to 2021 found prevalence declining among both mothers and daughters, with the decrease among daughters relative to mothers suggesting a generational shift possibly influenced by the Act.
energy_note: Two datasets, two directions, both recorded.

aspect: The obstetric consequence arrives fifteen years later
description: Types III and IV in particular complicate delivery, which routes back into MAT-001 and MAT-002 in the next generation.
energy_note: Cut at six, in obstructed labour at nineteen.

aspect: And it becomes an asylum claim that gets refused
description: The Canadian precedent in STA-001 denied a Nigerian woman's FGM-based claim on the basis she could have relocated to a large Nigerian city - so the same practice is both a recognised harm and an insufficient ground.
energy_note: Serious enough to be a human rights violation, not serious enough to be refuge.
